title: Intellectual property; problems of spreading and using information

learning_objectives.text: analyse problems arising due to disseminating and using information

lesson_objectives.all: define intellectual property and name the ways it is protected (copyright, patent, trademark) and the main software licences
lesson_objectives.most: explain piracy, plagiarism, misinformation and disinformation and decide whether an action is legal
lesson_objectives.some: analyse a real case of disseminating information: who is harmed, which right was broken and how to prevent it

assessment_criteria.criterion: Name ways of protecting intellectual property
descriptors: defines intellectual property, copyright, patent and trademark
states what each protects and how it is obtained
distinguishes proprietary, shareware, freeware, open-source and Creative Commons licences

assessment_criteria.criterion: Analyse problems of disseminating and using information
descriptors: identifies piracy, plagiarism, copyright infringement, mis- and disinformation
explains who is harmed and how
suggests legal and ethical ways to use information

learners_can: recommend actions with a reason (… should …, because …)
phrases: To use it legally, you should …

values.action: Learners discuss why citing sources and doing their own work is fair to classmates and authors.
Learners respect the work of creators — including Kazakh musicians, writers and developers — by paying for or crediting it.
Random groups share one laptop, agree on a case analysis and present it.

blocks.title: Hook: is it free?
blocks.teacher: Shows the objectives. Asks whether a photo found on Google may be used on the school website. The split vote leads into copyright.
blocks.learners: Vote on their laptops and justify their choice.

poll.question: A photo is found on Google Images. May the school put it on its website?
options: Yes — it is on the Internet, so it is free
Only if the author is named
Only with permission or a suitable licence (e.g. Creative Commons)

resources: Title slide: objectives and key words

blocks.title: Starter: recall last lesson
blocks.teacher: Opens three quick questions on the previous lesson and discusses the results.
blocks.learners: Answer individually; see their result at once.

blocks.title: Slides: intellectual property
blocks.teacher: Explains intellectual property, copyright, patent, trademark, industrial design and trade secret with Kazakh examples; then software licences and Creative Commons. Two votes during the slides.
blocks.learners: Take notes, vote on the together questions.

blocks.title: Pair work: protections and licences
blocks.teacher: Forms random pairs; walks round and helps.
blocks.learners: Work on the host's laptop and answer together.

blocks.title: Slides: problems of spreading and using information
blocks.teacher: Explains piracy, plagiarism, copyright infringement online, mis- and disinformation, disclosure of personal data; shows how to analyse a problem in five steps.

resources: Theory: Problems caused by disseminating and using information (slides)

blocks.teacher: Forms random groups of 4 and gives each a case card. Checks the analyses as they arrive; two groups present.
blocks.learners: Analyse the case in the labelled boxes on the host's laptop; present and answer one question from peers.

options: Not yet — I need more practice

ipp-l1-cases.details: A pupil bought a game once, then uploaded a cracked copy to a class chat. 40 classmates downloaded it; three laptops later showed adware.
A finalist's essay turned out to be copied almost word for word from a blog, with no quotation marks or reference.
Students used a popular song and photos found on Google in a video for the school's YouTube channel. The channel received a copyright strike.
A message "hot water with lemon cures flu — doctors hide it" spread through parents' chats; some parents stopped giving their children prescribed medicine.
A pupil posted a screenshot of the class list with names, phone numbers and home addresses in a public channel "as a joke".

live_tasks.title: Privacy policy
live_tasks.text: What must a privacy policy tell users?

options.content: What personal data is collected and how it is used

live_tasks.title: Malware
live_tasks.text: A program disguised as a free game opens a back door. It is a …

live_tasks.title: Unauthorised access
live_tasks.text: Using someone else's account without permission is …

live_tasks.title: Which protection?
live_tasks.text: A company invents a new type of phone battery. Which protection does the invention need?

options.content: A patent — it must be applied for and registered

scheme.explanation: Inventions are protected by a registered patent (about 20 years); copyright covers original works such as code, music and texts.

live_tasks.title: Freeware or open source?
live_tasks.text: A program is free and its source code can be read and changed. It is …

scheme.explanation: Freeware is free but closed; open source publishes the code and allows changes under its licence.

live_tasks.title: Spread by mistake
live_tasks.text: A pupil shares a false health tip, believing it is true. This is …

scheme.explanation: Misinformation is false information spread by mistake; disinformation is spread on purpose to deceive.

live_tasks.title: Case analysis: a problem of using information
live_tasks.text: Your group is the school's information-ethics board. Analyse the case on your card.

fields.label: Name the problem precisely (piracy, plagiarism, copyright infringement, misinformation, disclosure of personal data …)
What happened: how was the information copied, spread or used?
Who is harmed and how (at least two people or groups)
Which right or rule was broken (copyright, licence, consent, Law on Copyright of the RK …)
Two actions that would prevent it or put it right

scheme.mark_scheme:
Problem named correctly (1)
What happened described (1)
Two different groups harmed, each with the harm (2)
Right / rule broken identified (1)
Two sensible preventions or remedies, each linked to the problem (2)
Clear, well-argued analysis (1)
scheme.model_answer: Pirated game: copyright infringement / software piracy. A pupil copied a paid game and shared the download link in a chat. Harmed: the developers lose sales and money for updates; users risk malware and fines. Broken: copyright and the game's licence (Law on Copyright and Related Rights of the RK). Prevention: buy the licence or use a free / open-source alternative; remove the link and explain the risks to classmates.

live_tasks.title: Copyright
live_tasks.text: When does copyright on a pupil's original song begin?

options.content: Automatically when the song is created
Quoting a sentence in quotation marks and citing the author
Copying a paragraph from a website into an essay as your own words
Writing your own summary and listing the source
Using a CC BY photo and naming the author

live_tasks.title: Checking a source
live_tasks.text: Before sharing a surprising news story, the best first step is to …

options.content: share it quickly so friends know
check who published it and compare with other reliable sources
